title: A Package Tour
description: Take an offer apart before it takes your money, then write back. The words of a journey in four families — Accommodation (full board, single room, camp site, to check in), Means of transport (coach, jet, passenger, return ticket), Tourism (package tour, journey, travel agent) and Sightseeing (monument, temple, palace, statue) — with journey, trip, tour and travel kept apart. How an ad persuades: it speaks to you, names the benefit instead of the feature, piles up what is free and ends with an instruction. How you read one back: what exactly is included, what the asterisk takes away (not included, extra, a separate ticket is required), what you must still do, and what the page never printed at all — because a promise is not information, admission is the right to enter, a discount lowers a price without removing it, and several is not a figure. Then weigh a package tour, one price and everything arranged against a programme somebody else fixed, and give an opinion whose reason comes out of the ad itself. Say that the offer attracts you with the five frames and the slot each one needs (X sounds interesting, I'm interested in X, I'd like to know more about X, Please tell me about X, I'm keen on X), never confusing interested with interesting, and write the e-mail: a subject line that names the request, four moves from where you saw the offer to Yours faithfully, no question the ad has already answered, and the referring words that hold the message together. Hear the two vowels behind it all — the stressed [æ] of package, access and capital, and the weak schwa [ə] of festival, announced and the adjective separate — and build your own festival page in Project Work 1
